note: Taal: the idiom bank. One featured idiom per day rotating nl, fr, it. The run appends one entry per day and never repeats a phrase. The page shows today's and a review line (yesterday, a week ago, a month ago).

idioms.phrase: de kat uit de boom kijken
idioms.literal: to watch the cat out of the tree
idioms.meaning: to wait and see how things develop before committing
idioms.example: Bij de begrotingsonderhandelingen kijkt de oppositie eerst de kat uit de boom.
idioms.note: Very common in political reporting; the Belgian form is the same.

idioms.literal: to have other cats to whip
idioms.meaning: to have more important things to do
idioms.example: Le bourgmestre n'a pas répondu : il a d'autres chats à fouetter.
idioms.note: Used across Wallonia and France; the English cousin is 'bigger fish to fry'.

idioms.literal: into the mouth of the wolf
idioms.meaning: good luck (said before an exam, a match or a journey)
idioms.example: Domani hai l'esame? In bocca al lupo!
idioms.note: The reply is 'crepi (il lupo)', may the wolf die; never answer 'grazie'.

idioms.literal: to put water in the wine
idioms.meaning: to compromise; to settle for less than you first asked
idioms.example: Als het kabinet op 12 november een meerderheid wil, zal het water bij de wijn moeten doen.
idioms.register: neutral; heard daily in politics and in meetings
idioms.note: The standard phrase for coalition bargaining, so expect it all week around the tax-plan vote. A colleague who says 'we moeten allebei wat water bij de wijn doen' is offering a deal, not a lecture.

idioms.phrase: mettre la charrue avant les bœufs
idioms.literal: to put the plough before the oxen
idioms.meaning: to do things in the wrong order; to decide before the groundwork is done
idioms.example: Signer le contrat avant d'avoir vu le devis, c'est mettre la charrue avant les bœufs.
idioms.note: The English cousin is 'to put the cart before the horse'. Heard in meetings when someone wants a decision before the facts are in; the negative form, 'il ne faut pas mettre la charrue avant les bœufs', is the usual brake.

idioms.literal: to have your hands in the dough
idioms.meaning: to be involved in something from the inside, often with the contacts to steer it; to have a finger in the pie
idioms.example: Nel nuovo progetto ha le mani in pasta anche il ministero, quindi conviene parlarne prima con loro.
idioms.register: everyday, all of Italy; neutral to slightly informal
idioms.note: It can be admiring (someone who knows how things work) or suspicious (someone with too many interests). The stronger form, 'avere le mani in pasta dappertutto', means to be involved in everything.

idioms.phrase: met de deur in huis vallen
idioms.literal: to fall into the house with the door
idioms.meaning: to come straight to the point, without preamble or small talk
idioms.example: Ik val maar meteen met de deur in huis: het budget voor volgend jaar is te krap.
idioms.register: neutral; common at work and at home
idioms.note: Often used to announce your own directness: “Ik val maar met de deur in huis” (I'll get straight to the point). Dutch meetings tend to open this way, which can sound abrupt to American ears.

idioms.phrase: se faire rouler dans la farine
idioms.literal: to get rolled in the flour
idioms.meaning: to be taken in, conned or made a fool of
idioms.example: Avec ce faux site de réservation, beaucoup de touristes se sont fait rouler dans la farine.
idioms.register: familiar; everyday speech and the press
idioms.note: Rouler quelqu'un already means to cheat someone; the flour adds the picture of being dusted white and left looking foolish. In the passé composé the participle stays fait: elle s'est fait rouler, not faite.

idioms.meaning: to pretend not to hear; to ignore a request or a warning on purpose
idioms.example: Abbiamo chiesto tre volte una risposta scritta, ma il fornitore continua a fare orecchie da mercante.
idioms.register: neutral; everyday speech and the press, common in political reporting
idioms.note: The picture is the market trader who hears only what suits the sale. Close to the English 'to turn a deaf ear'; the verb conjugates normally (fa orecchie da mercante, hanno fatto orecchie da mercante), and the noun never takes an article.
